claims.text: The starting material is a W–Cu composite with tungsten particles or interconnected tungsten ligaments embedded in a copper matrix.
Tungsten surfaces should be coated with an ultra-thin reactive Ti-based coating or Ti/Ni bilayer before composite consolidation.
The interfacial coating physically separates the tungsten phase from the copper matrix.
The Ti-based or Ti/Ni coating functions as a diffusion barrier at the W/Cu interface.
The coating reduces interdiffusion between tungsten and copper.
The coating accommodates the thermal-expansion mismatch between tungsten and copper.
Reduced interdiffusion and accommodation of thermal-expansion mismatch mitigate phase-separated regions.
Reduced interdiffusion and accommodation of thermal-expansion mismatch mitigate interfacial void formation.
The coated W–Cu composite will have higher thermal conductivity than an otherwise identical uncoated composite.
The coated composite will have a lower frequency of interfacial void formation than the uncoated composite.
Untreated W–Cu composites are prone to phase separation under the stated service conditions.
Untreated W–Cu composites are prone to interfacial void formation under the stated service conditions.
The proposed benefit applies during conventional composite consolidation.
The proposed benefit persists under cyclic high-heat-flux and irradiation conditions relevant to W-based plasma-facing material/Cu-based cooling-component joints.
Analogous surface and interfacial engineering strategies have improved bonding in other composite systems.
The magnitude of any thermal-conductivity improvement under combined high heat flux and irradiation is uncertain.
